habitat: A tree of cool, humid country, where July averages 65 to 74°F. It grows on almost any soil, but competes best on well-drained sands and gravels, where it once formed vast stands; it also takes rocky ridges and the edges of bogs. Young trees grow well in partial shade.
distribution: Across southern Canada from Newfoundland and the Gaspé west to Ontario and southeastern Manitoba; south through the Great Lakes states, New England and New York to Pennsylvania and New Jersey, and along the Appalachians to northern Georgia. A variety grows in the mountains of southern Mexico and Guatemala.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Mostly the rich, moist bottomlands of river valleys and limestone soils, in climates from subhumid in the west to humid in the east. It is hardy to −20 to −30°F, though southern seed sources planted in the north suffer frost damage. Planted, it puts up with drought, road salt, compacted soil and city heat, which is how it reached northern streets.
distribution: Scattered through the east-central United States, from central Pennsylvania west to southeastern South Dakota and south to Texas and Alabama; at its biggest in the valleys of small streams in southern Indiana and Illinois. It has run wild east of the Appalachians as far as New York and New England, and the thornless form is planted in temperate countries around the world.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: It grows best on deep, moist, well-drained loams on north- and east-facing slopes and in coves, but is common on drier ridges too, in climates from 30 inches of rain a year in the northwest of its range to 80 in the southern Appalachians, and from 100 frost-free days in the north to 220 in the south. Its seedlings stand moderate shade and shoot up when a gap opens in the canopy.
distribution: The only native oak that reaches Nova Scotia: from Cape Breton, Prince Edward Island and the Gaspé west through Ontario to Minnesota, and south to eastern Nebraska, Oklahoma, Alabama, Georgia and North Carolina, with outliers in Louisiana and Mississippi.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A tree of alluvial soils along rivers, streams and the edges of swamps, on ground that floods in spring, often rich in clay; now and then it takes hold on dry ground. It is most abundant in the hot, humid Southeast, with 50 inches of rain and over 200 frost-free days a year. It needs sun, and acid soil: on alkaline ground its leaves turn yellow.
distribution: Mainly the southeastern quarter of the United States, from eastern Texas and southeastern Iowa to Virginia and northern Florida, with scattered stands along rivers north to southern Minnesota, central Wisconsin and southern New England. It is absent from most of the Appalachians and the lower coastal plain, and from limestone country in Missouri, Tennessee and Kentucky.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Fast-growing, it copes with a wide range of soils, shade, drought and city pollution, but does best in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained soils, often at the foot of hills where water runs in; it is rare on very acid ground. Its seedlings sprout and grow in shade, even under a closed canopy, and the tree needs more light as it matures. In North American woods its seedlings come up thickly under its own crown.
distribution: The most widespread native maple in Europe, from Greece, the Balkans, northern Italy and the Pyrenees north to southern Scandinavia and east into Russia, short of the Urals, from sea level to 4,600 feet in the Alps. It is not native to western France, the British Isles, the Netherlands or Denmark. A subspecies grows in the mountains of Turkey, the Caucasus and northern Iran, and the range map shows outlying stands in Central Asia. Brought to the United States in the 1700s, it has gone wild in parts of the East.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: A tree of wet ground: poorly drained flats, river bottoms, the edges of swamps and lakes, mucks and peats where the water table stands high, in country with 25 to 50 inches of rain a year and winters down to −30°F. It grows scattered among other trees rather than in stands.
distribution: From southwestern Maine and southern Quebec west through New York, Ontario and Michigan to southeastern Minnesota, and south to Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia and New Jersey. It is most common, and grows biggest, in western New York and northern Ohio.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Cool, humid mountain country with most of its rain in summer and as few as 55 to 60 frost-free days a year, mostly along streams and on moist slopes in mountain valleys between about 6,000 and 11,000 feet, seldom in stands of its own. Planted, it does best in full sun and well-drained soil.
distribution: Wild only in the central and southern Rocky Mountains, from western Wyoming and eastern Idaho south through Utah and Colorado to Arizona and New Mexico, with a few isolated stands reported in north-central Montana.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: It grows on a wider range of soils, moisture and elevations than probably any other tree in North America, from dry ridges and south-facing slopes to peat bogs and swamps. It does best on moist, moderately well-drained ground at low to middle elevations, in sun or part shade. In New England it grows both on dry, rocky uplands and in nearly pure stands along swamp edges; in the far South it is almost wholly a swamp tree. Its seedlings have come through two months of flooding unharmed.
distribution: One of the most abundant and widespread trees of eastern North America, from southern Newfoundland and Quebec west to southeastern Manitoba and northern Minnesota, and south to eastern Texas and Florida. Of any tree in Florida, it has the longest continuous range along the Atlantic coast, some 1,600 miles. Its northern limit follows the line where winter lows reach −40°F; it is missing from the prairies of the Midwest.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Mountains from about 1,150 feet in Italy to 7,200 in the Taurus of Turkey, best between 2,600 and 4,900 feet, on soils from sandy podzols to limestone; Austrian pine in particular takes exposed chalk and limestone. It stands drought, wind, both very dry and humid places and big swings in temperature, and needs light, though it takes more shade than Scots pine.
distribution: A fragmented range, shrunk by a warming climate and people over thousands of years: from northwestern Africa through southern Europe, from Spain, Corsica and Austria through the Balkans, to Crimea, Turkey and Cyprus.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Level, poorly drained floodplains and river bottoms with clay soils that flood in the dormant season but seldom in summer; it avoids the very lowest, wettest ground. It needs acid soil, and grows fast in full sun. Its climate runs from humid to moist subhumid, with 32 to over 50 inches of rain a year.
distribution: From southwestern New England west to extreme southern Ontario, southern Michigan, northern Illinois and Iowa; south to Missouri, eastern Kansas and northeastern Oklahoma; and east through Arkansas and Tennessee to central North Carolina and Virginia.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Only in cool, moist climates, with January averaging about 0°F in the north of its range and 50°F in the south, and 20 to 80 inches of rain a year. At its best on deep, moist, fertile, well-drained loams, where it often dominates the forest with beech and yellow birch. Its seedlings stand deep shade and can wait decades under the canopy for a gap.
distribution: Its northern limit runs from the southeast corner of Manitoba through central Ontario and southern Quebec to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. In the United States it grows throughout New England, New York and Pennsylvania, south along the Appalachians to Tennessee, and west to Missouri, eastern Iowa and eastern Minnesota, with a few outliers in Kansas, Georgia and the Carolinas.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: It grows in two very different places: cedar swamps on wet, often limy peat, and dry limestone ledges and cliffs, in climates averaging 39 to 50°F a year with 30 to 40 inches of rain. Some peatlands in Michigan may have held it continuously for 8,500 years.
distribution: From the Atlantic coast in Nova Scotia and Maine west to Manitoba and Minnesota. The southern edge of its main range crosses central New York and central Michigan, with isolated stands south along the Appalachians to North Carolina. Fire limits it in the north and west, and heat in the south.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A tough, adaptable tree that grows in extreme climates and on many soils, best on moist, well-drained loams. At the northern tree line it stops roughly where July averages 50°F.
distribution: Across the continent, from Newfoundland and Labrador west along the northern limit of trees to Hudson Bay, the Northwest Territories, Yukon and Alaska, almost reaching the Arctic Ocean at 69°N near the Mackenzie delta. In the east it comes south to northern Minnesota and Wisconsin, central Michigan, the Adirondacks and Maine.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A tree of lowlands and lower hill slopes, in mixed broadleaf woods on fertile soils, up to about 4,900 feet in the central Alps. It has grown in European woods for over 10,000 years; in England, where it grows with oak and beech, it marks ancient woodland.
distribution: The more abundant of Europe's two native lindens, centred on central and eastern Europe, from southern Norway and Finland south to Italy and east to the Caucasus, and beyond the Urals into western Siberia. It does not reach Europe's far west: its western limits are in northwestern Spain and Wales.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: The main tree of Europe's northern and subalpine conifer forests, from sea level in the north to above 7,800 feet in the Alps, where it grows stunted. It stands shade, surviving for decades under a closed canopy, but dislikes salt wind, summer drought and waterlogged ground.
distribution: From the mountains of central Europe north and east through Scandinavia and northern and eastern Europe to the Urals and beyond into western Siberia, where it merges with Siberian spruce, sometimes counted as a subspecies of it.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Along streams and in moist valleys on rich soils. Planted, it does best in full sun, on almost any well-drained soil, acid or alkaline, and once established stands drought and wind.
distribution: Wild in Japan, Korea, eastern China and Taiwan.

habitat: Planted, it takes full sun and almost any soil, clay to sand, acid or alkaline, wet or dry.
distribution: Almost every ginkgo alive was planted. Whether any truly wild ones remain is debated: the likeliest are scattered trees in the mountains of southwestern China, which some think were kept alive by Buddhist monks for centuries.

habitat: Cold winters, warm summers and a humid to subhumid climate, at its best where July averages 65 to 80°F. It grows on moist, deep, fertile soils of slopes and valleys, mixed with sugar maple, elms and ashes rather than in stands, and sprouts readily from a cut stump.
distribution: From southwestern New Brunswick and New England west through Quebec and Ontario to the southeast corner of Manitoba; south through the eastern Dakotas, Nebraska and Kansas to northeastern Oklahoma; and east through northern Arkansas and Tennessee to western North Carolina and New Jersey.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A tree of riverbanks and floodplains, where it stands spring floods for weeks better than the trees around it; in the drier parts of its range it grows only along streams. It is missing from cold high mountains. In Vermont it dominates the floodplain forests along the big rivers and the shores of Lake Champlain.
distribution: From New Brunswick, central Maine and southern Quebec west through Ontario and Michigan to Minnesota and southeastern South Dakota; south to Kansas and Oklahoma; and east through Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama to northwestern Florida and central Georgia. Planted on Russia's Black Sea coast, it has gone wild there in small stands.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A northern tree of cold climates: it seldom grows wild where July averages above 70°F, and in the south of its range keeps to cool north slopes and high mountains. A pioneer, it seeds into ground opened by fire, logging or clearing, in full sun, and gives way in time to trees that stand more shade.
distribution: Its range follows the northern limit of trees from Newfoundland and Labrador west across the continent to northwest Alaska, south along the Pacific to Washington and into the northern Rockies, and east through Minnesota and the Great Lakes to New England, reaching down the Appalachians to western North Carolina.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Best on rich, moist ground along streams, in bottomlands and on lower slopes, in the shade of taller hardwoods, though it tolerates a wide variety of sites, and climates from 28 inches of rain a year in Minnesota to 62 on the Gulf Coast. It stands more shade than almost any tree it grows among.
distribution: Most of the eastern United States, into southwestern Quebec and southeastern Ontario, and west just past the Mississippi to the Ozarks and eastern Texas. It is missing from the lower Mississippi bottomlands, most of Florida, the New Jersey pine barrens, Cape Cod and the White and Adirondack Mountains. It also grows in central and southern Mexico, Guatemala and western Honduras.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Forest edges, old fields and thickets, and young woods coming back on cleared land. Planted, it does best in full sun to part shade, on almost any soil, even shallow and rocky, acid or alkaline.
distribution: Native to the eastern United States, chiefly the Southeast and the lower Midwest. In New England, Vermont included, it grows only where planted.
source: Go Botany (Native Plant Trust); NC State Extension

habitat: Mixed forests, valleys and gullies, from near sea level into the mountains. Planted, it does best in full sun, in moist, well-drained, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild in northern Japan, mostly Hokkaido, and in Korea, northern China and the far southeast of Russia.

habitat: Almost always on bottomlands and along streams, on alluvial soils, where it grows faster than nearly any hardwood and reaches its largest size. It is often among the first trees on new ground left by a river. Its range is probably held back by frost in the north and by the dry Great Plains in the west.
distribution: Every state east of the Great Plains except Minnesota: from southwestern Maine west through New York, southern Ontario and Michigan to southern Wisconsin, Iowa and eastern Nebraska, and south to eastern Kansas, Oklahoma, south-central Texas, northwestern Florida and southeastern Georgia. It also grows in the mountains of northeastern Mexico.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Open, disturbed ground in full sun, in a humid climate with 150 to 210 frost-free days in its native range.
distribution: Its original range is not known exactly: two separate areas, one in the Appalachians from central Pennsylvania and southern Ohio to northeastern Alabama, northern Georgia and northwestern South Carolina, the other in the Ozark Plateau and Ouachita Mountains of Missouri, Arkansas and Oklahoma. Planted widely, it has run wild across the United States and southern Canada and in parts of Europe and Asia.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Moist broadleaf forests in a warm-temperate climate, above all the bottoms of shady ravines over limestone and alluvial soils, with hornbeam, and mixed mountain forests up to 5,200 feet. Its seeds die if they dry out, so seedlings cannot take hold on open, dry ground.
distribution: A relic of the ice ages, wild now only in two small ranges: the mountains of Greece, Albania and North Macedonia, and the Preslav Balkan in Bulgaria. Seed brought from Turkey to Prague in 1557 began its planting across Europe; the trees of streets and parks in Europe and North America all descend from planted ones.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: A main tree of Europe's temperate broadleaf forests, with a wide tolerance but at its best on fertile, moist soils, including heavy clays and river floodplains, where it dominates at low to middle elevations. It needs sun, though its big acorns let seedlings survive among grass while their roots go deep. Leafing out late, it seldom suffers late frost.
distribution: Most of Europe, north to the Norwegian coast and northern Scotland, south to Portugal, southern Italy, Greece and southern Turkey, and east into central Russia as far as the Urals; up to about 4,300 feet in the Alps.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Swamps, river bottoms and lake edges that flood off and on, where drainage matters more than rainfall; it grows in climates from 30 to 64 inches of rain a year and from 190 frost-free days in southern Illinois to almost all year in southern Florida. Planted in the open it does well on ordinary soil, and is hardy far north of where it grows wild.
distribution: The lower Atlantic coastal plain from southern Delaware to southern Florida, and along the Gulf coast to southeastern Texas. Inland, it follows streams up the coastal plain and the Mississippi Valley to southeastern Oklahoma, southeastern Missouri, southern Illinois and southwestern Indiana.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: One of the most drought-resistant North American oaks, growing where rain is as scant as 15 inches a year and the season only 100 days long. It grows on river bottoms, dry uplands and the savannas between forest and prairie, where its thick bark let it survive the grass fires that kept other trees out. It does best in southern Illinois and Indiana.
distribution: Across the East and the Great Plains, from southern New Brunswick, Maine, Vermont and southern Quebec west through Ontario to southern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan; south through the Dakotas, northeastern Wyoming and Nebraska to western Oklahoma and southeastern Texas; and northeast through Arkansas, Tennessee and West Virginia to Pennsylvania and Connecticut.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Planted, it does best in full sun to part shade, in well-drained loam.
distribution: Wild in northern Japan, mostly Hokkaido and northern Honshu, and in Korea, Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and the far southeast of Russia: the coldest homeland of any of the ornamental cherries.
source: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew); NC State Extension

habitat: A cultivated form that grows wild nowhere, kept going from cuttings. Its species, the black poplar, grows along rivers and on floodplains, on wet sand and gravel that floods.
distribution: The black poplar is wild from Europe and northwest Africa to central Asia.

habitat: Bottomland woods along streams and the foot of bluffs. Planted far beyond its range for its flowers and fast growth, it has run wild in old fields and along fencerows. Planted, it does well in full sun to part shade, in clay or loam.
distribution: Native to a small area of the central Mississippi valley, from southern Illinois and Indiana to Arkansas and western Tennessee; now naturalized across much of the East.
source: Missouri Department of Conservation; NC State Extension

habitat: Above all well-drained, acid soils of ridges and upper slopes. It survives there now mostly as sprouts from old root systems.
distribution: Before the blight it was among the commonest trees of the Appalachian forest, from Maine and southern Ontario to Georgia and Mississippi.

habitat: A wide variety of climates. The coast form grows in the Pacific Northwest's mild, wet winters and cool, fairly dry summers, among the tallest trees in the world; the inland form is smaller and hardier, and stands colder, harsher winters, which is why the trees planted in the Northeast are mostly that one.
distribution: The greatest north–south range of any western timber conifer, from 19° to 55°N, shaped like an upside-down V. From central British Columbia, the coast form runs south through the Pacific Coast Ranges to southern California; the Rocky Mountain form runs nearly 2,800 miles down the Rockies into the mountains of central Mexico.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A light-demanding pioneer of sunny to partly shaded, usually poor ground, from dry sands to rocky slopes, that colonizes newly disturbed sites. With strong drought tolerance and frost resistance, it asks very little of its soil or water.
distribution: The most widespread pine in the world, and the second most widespread conifer after common juniper: from Spain to the far east of Russia, and from northern Scandinavia at 70°N to Spain's Sierra Nevada at 37°N, from sea level in the north to over 8,500 feet in the Caucasus. Widely planted in the United States, especially the Northeast and the Lake States.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Scattered through hardwood forests, alone or in small groups, rarely in stands of its own. It grows best on deep, rich, moist but well-drained ground in coves and bottoms, needs sun, and does best where the year averages about 55°F with at least 170 frost-free days.
distribution: The central and eastern United States, from western Vermont and Massachusetts west through New York, southern Ontario and central Michigan to southern Minnesota, eastern South Dakota and Nebraska; south to western Oklahoma and central Texas; and east, skipping the lower Mississippi valley and delta, to northwestern Florida and Georgia.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Mostly a small understory tree of open woods, woodland edges, rocky slopes and stream banks, on sites from dry to moist, though it grows better on moist ground. Its range spans climates from 20 inches of rain a year in south Texas to 50 in central Florida.
distribution: From New Jersey and southern Pennsylvania northwest to southern Michigan, southwest to southeastern Nebraska, south to central Texas and east to central Florida. A separate population runs from the Trans-Pecos and south Texas into Mexico.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Many kinds of ground, but best on deep, moist, well-drained soils, in climates from winters of −50°F in Minnesota to mild north Florida, and from 30 to 80 inches of rain a year. It is long-lived, slow-growing and moderately shade-tolerant.
distribution: Most of the eastern United States, from southwestern Maine and southern Quebec west through Ontario and Michigan to southeastern Minnesota; south to western Iowa, eastern Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas; and east to northern Florida and Georgia. It is absent from the high Appalachians and the Mississippi delta. The best growing conditions are on the west slopes of the Appalachians and in the Ohio and central Mississippi valleys, but the largest trees have been found on the Eastern Shore of Delaware and Maryland.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Cool, humid places with soil that stays moist through the growing season: ravines, north-facing slopes, stream banks and rocky ridges; in the southern Appalachians it keeps to higher, cooler north slopes. It stands more shade than almost any other tree in its range.
distribution: Eastern North America from about 33° to 48°N, from Nova Scotia and the Great Lakes south along the Appalachians to Georgia and Alabama, yet on less than a tenth of the region's forest land, where the microclimate is cool and moist. Its present range limits took shape only 1,000 to 2,000 years ago.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: At its best in the deep, moist, well-drained soils of Appalachian coves and lower slopes, in climates from New England winters to almost frost-free central Florida, with 30 to 80 inches of rain a year. It grows fast and needs sun, so it fills gaps and old fields. In Vermont it is rare.
distribution: The eastern United States from southern New England west through southern Ontario and Michigan, south to Louisiana and east to north-central Florida. It grows most abundantly, and largest, in the Ohio River valley and on the mountain slopes of North Carolina, Tennessee, Kentucky and West Virginia.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Mixed broadleaf forests on lowlands and hills. Its tolerance of heat and dry summers comes from there. Planted, it does best in full sun to part shade, in moist, well-drained loam, neutral to alkaline.
distribution: Wild in southeastern Europe and western Asia, from Hungary, Romania and the Balkans east to northwestern Turkey.

habitat: Valleys and streamsides in the mountains, mostly in or beside rice paddies and villages. Very few of the wild trees remain. Planted, it does best in full sun, in moist, rich, acid to neutral soil.
distribution: Wild only in a small area of central China, on the borders of Hubei, Hunan and Chongqing.

habitat: A tree of bottomlands and moist slopes, in climates with 40 to 60 inches of rain a year and 180 to 320 frost-free days; it also seeds fast into old fields and cutover land.
distribution: From Connecticut south through the East to central Florida and eastern Texas, and west to Missouri, Arkansas, Oklahoma and southern Illinois. It also grows in scattered places in Mexico and Central America, from Guatemala and Belize to Nicaragua.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Rich, moist, well-drained soils, often with sugar maple and yellow birch in the northern hardwood forest, with 30 to 50 inches of rain a year: it uses about twice as much water as some drought-resistant oaks. It stands deep shade, and spreads by suckers from its roots into thickets of young beech.
distribution: From Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, west through Maine, southern Quebec and Ontario to northern Michigan and eastern Wisconsin; south to southern Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas, southeastern Oklahoma and eastern Texas; and east to northern Florida and South Carolina. A variety grows in the mountains of northeastern Mexico.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Dry, rocky, sunny hillsides and open woods, often on limestone. Planted, it does best in full sun, on almost any well-drained soil, even shallow and rocky.
distribution: Wild from southern Europe across the Caucasus and the Himalaya to central China.

habitat: Woods, woodland edges and old hedgerows, on chalk and limestone as well as heavy clays. Planted, it does best in full sun, on clay, loam or sand, and stands some dryness.
distribution: Wild across most of Europe, north to southern Scandinavia, and in North Africa and western Asia.

habitat: An understory tree of dry, well-drained slopes and ridges, on a wide variety of soils, in climates from 18 inches of rain and 100 frost-free days in the northwest of its range to 64 inches and 290 days on the Gulf coast. It grows slowly in the shade of oaks and maples.
distribution: Most of the eastern half of the United States, from Cape Breton and Prince Edward Island west through southern Ontario and northern Michigan to southeastern Manitoba, the Dakotas and northeastern Wyoming, and south to Florida and Texas. It also grows in the mountains of Mexico, south to El Salvador and Honduras.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Notable in the cypress family for how well it stands cool, wet conditions: cool, humid mountain forests, mostly at middle and upper elevations, with deep snow and short growing seasons. It stands poor, wet soils.
distribution: From northern California to Prince William Sound in Alaska, nearly all within 100 miles of the Pacific coast; in Oregon and Washington in the Cascades and the Olympic Mountains. Isolated stands in the Siskiyou Mountains near the Oregon border mark its southern limit.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Sandy and gravelly uplands, in climates from the Atlantic coast's marine air to the continental cold of Minnesota, with humid summers and 20 to 60 inches of rain a year. It needs full sun and comes in fast after fire or cutting, mostly by suckers from the roots of the trees that were there.
distribution: The northeastern and north-central United States and southeastern Canada, from Cape Breton Island west to southeastern Manitoba, south through Minnesota and Iowa to northeastern Missouri, and east to southern Illinois, Kentucky, Virginia and Delaware. It is most abundant in southwestern Quebec and southeastern Ontario.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Moist bottomlands and slopes, old fields and open woods.
distribution: Wild in the lower Midwest and the upper South, from Pennsylvania west to Kansas and south to Tennessee and Arkansas.

habitat: Cool places with abundant rain, on cool, moist, well-drained soils of slopes and stream banks, with sugar maple, beech and hemlock in the northern hardwood forest. Its northern limit follows the line where the year averages 35°F. Its seedlings take root on rotting logs and mossy stumps.
distribution: From Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick west through southern Ontario to southeastern Manitoba; south to Minnesota and northeastern Iowa; east through Ohio and Pennsylvania to New Jersey and New England; and down the Appalachians to Tennessee and Georgia, where it keeps to moist gorges above 3,000 feet. The largest stands of it are in Quebec.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Poor, dry, sandy or gravelly ground and abandoned fields, where it is among the first trees to come in after fire or clearing.
distribution: Wild from Nova Scotia and southern Quebec to Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

habitat: A small understory tree of moist woods, stream banks and the edges of swamps, and of dry rocky bluffs.
distribution: Wild in the eastern United States from Massachusetts south to Florida and west to Oklahoma and Texas.

habitat: Moist forests along mountain streams, where old trees grow to great size, often with several trunks.
distribution: Wild in Japan and China.

habitat: It forms forests of its own on well-drained soils, especially chalk and limestone, and needs a growing season of at least 140 days; summer heat and drought limit it, and in the south of its range it grows only above about 3,300 feet. Its dense shade keeps almost anything else from growing beneath it.
distribution: From Sicily north to Bergen in southern Norway, and from the Cantabrian Mountains of Spain east to the Carpathians and the Balkans, though not on the Po plain or the Hungarian plain. Farther east, in a more continental climate, the oriental beech takes over, in northern Turkey, the Caucasus and northern Iran.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Thickets, forest edges and mountain woods; where it has run wild, old fields, roadsides and woodland edges.
distribution: Wild in China, Korea and Taiwan. Planted across North America, it has run wild in much of the East.

habitat: Mostly rich, moist bottomlands and lower slopes. It spreads by suckers, so a stand is often one tree's clones.
distribution: Wild but scattered and nowhere common, from western New York and southern Ontario to Nebraska and Oklahoma.

habitat: A small understory tree of mountain forests and thickets.
distribution: Wild in Japan, Korea and China.

habitat: A cultivated tree, found wild only where it has escaped.
distribution: Its main ancestor, the wild apple Malus sieversii, still grows in the mountain forests of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, in the Tian Shan.

habitat: Mixed forests on slopes and along streams.
distribution: Wild in the mountains of northeastern China and Korea.

habitat: Most often on moist ground, along riverbanks, floodplains and lake shores, yet drought-tolerant enough to be planted in windbreaks across the Plains, and it can survive long flooding. It also seeds fast into vacant lots, rail yards and old fields. Planted trees grow as far north as Fort Simpson in the Northwest Territories.
distribution: The most widely distributed of all North American maples, from coast to coast and from Canada to Guatemala: in the East from New York to central Florida and southern Texas, northwest through the Plains to Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and in the West along watercourses in the Rockies, the Colorado Plateau and California.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Along streams and on moist, rich slopes in coves, in a climate that is humid, or superhumid in the southern Appalachians, with 40 to over 80 inches of rain spread through the year.
distribution: Mostly the Piedmont and mountains of the Carolinas, eastern Tennessee, Georgia and Alabama, with small scattered populations from the southeastern coastal plain north to West Virginia, southern Ohio, Indiana and Illinois and west to Arkansas and southeastern Oklahoma.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: An understory tree of open hardwood and pine forests, on moist, well-drained, acid soils, in climates from 30 inches of rain a year in the north to 80 in the southern Appalachians.
distribution: From extreme southwestern Maine west through New York, southern Ontario and Michigan to central Illinois and Missouri; south to southeastern Kansas, eastern Oklahoma and east Texas; and east to northern Florida. A variety grows in the mountains of Nuevo León and Veracruz, Mexico. In Vermont it grows wild only in the south of the state.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Mostly limestone cliffs and ridges, and the rich soils of coves and stream banks.
distribution: Rare and scattered in the wild, from western North Carolina west to eastern Oklahoma, and from southern Missouri and Indiana south to central Alabama.

habitat: Mixed forests on mountain slopes, where it is now rare.
distribution: Wild only in central China.

habitat: Most often river bottoms and floodplains, but also dry, rocky limestone ridges. It stands great extremes: from 14 inches of rain a year on the Great Plains, where temperatures swing 140°F or more over a year, to 60 inches in the Southeast.
distribution: Widely across the eastern United States, from southern New England and central New York west through southern Ontario to the Dakotas, with outliers in southern Quebec, Manitoba and Wyoming; south to northeastern Colorado and northwestern Texas, and east to Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Mixed forests along rivers and on mountain slopes. Planted in the Northeast, it seeds into nearby woods.
distribution: Wild in northeastern China, Korea, Japan and the Russian Far East.

habitat: Moist bottomlands and stream banks, though like most trees it grows best on fertile, moist, well-drained soil. Its climate runs from subhumid to humid, with 15 to 60 inches of rain a year and 120 to 280 frost-free days.
distribution: The most widespread ash in North America, from Cape Breton Island and Nova Scotia west to southeastern Alberta, and south through Montana and Wyoming to southeastern Texas and east to northwestern Florida and Georgia. Planted along streets across the continent, it is now dying everywhere the emerald ash borer has reached.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Mountain forests, in moist, rich soils, often near streams.
distribution: Wild in Japan and Korea.

habitat: One of the least demanding trees, cold-hardy and frost-tolerant, on thin, acid soils, rocky ground and the edges of woods, but not wetlands, bare ground, clays or soft limestone. It is suited to a short growing season, and held back by drought more than by heat; in the south of its range it grows only high in the mountains.
distribution: Across Europe from Iceland, Scandinavia and northern Russia south to Spain, Italy and the Balkans, and, the range map shows, east across northern Asia to the Pacific coast of Russia.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Cool, moist ground from swamps to mountain slopes, at its best where the year averages 35 to 40°F with 30 to 43 inches of rain. With red spruce it makes up the dark forest of Vermont's higher mountains.
distribution: Across the northern forest from Newfoundland and Labrador west through Quebec and Ontario to the Peace River in northwestern Alberta; in the United States, from northern Minnesota through Wisconsin and Michigan to northern New England and the Adirondacks, with outliers in the Appalachians. It grows best in southeastern Canada and the Northeast.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: High mountains with long winters, moderate to heavy snowpack, short growing seasons and 20 to 35 inches of rain a year in the Rockies; in California it also grows in warmer, drier country. Its thick-barked, drought-hardened trees are why it copes with eastern summers.
distribution: The mountains of the West, from the Pacific coast ranges to central Colorado, and from central Oregon and southeastern Idaho south to northern Mexico.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A wide range of climates; at its best on the deep, moist soils of the Allegheny Plateau of Pennsylvania and New York, where the climate is cool and moist with 38 to 44 inches of rain spread through the year. A tree of the northern hardwood forest, it also seeds into old fields and fencerows, carried by birds.
distribution: From Nova Scotia and New Brunswick west through southern Quebec and Ontario to Michigan and eastern Minnesota; south to Iowa, eastern Nebraska, Oklahoma and Texas; and east to central Florida. Its varieties reach Arizona, and south through Mexico to Guatemala.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Moist, well-drained slopes and coves, often with hemlock, sugar maple and yellow birch, where about 45 inches of rain falls a year and, in the north, 80 to 100 inches of snow.
distribution: Mainly the northeastern United States, from southern Maine west through southern Quebec, New Hampshire, Vermont, New York and southeastern Ontario to eastern Ohio, and south through Pennsylvania along the Appalachians to northern Alabama and Georgia. It is most abundant in Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York and Pennsylvania. In Vermont it grows wild mostly in the south and the Champlain Valley.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A tree of southern river bottoms: floodplains and bottomland ridges on ground that floods only briefly, in a humid climate of hot summers, short mild winters and 50 to 60 inches of rain a year.
distribution: Along the Atlantic coastal plain from New Jersey and eastern Pennsylvania to northern Florida and west to east Texas, and north up the Mississippi valley to southeastern Oklahoma, Arkansas, Missouri, southern Illinois and Indiana, and locally Kentucky and Tennessee.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Moist, cool forests on mountain slopes.
distribution: Wild in the mountains of central and southern Japan, where it was long reserved for temples and palaces. It is still among the most planted timber trees in Japan.

habitat: An understory tree of rich, moist ravines and slopes, sheltered from the wind that would shred its huge leaves.
distribution: Wild but scattered in the Southeast, from Ohio and Kentucky to Louisiana and Georgia.

habitat: Where it has run wild: fencerows, vacant lots and woodland edges. It hybridizes with the native red mulberry.
distribution: Wild in northern China, and grown across Asia for millennia to feed silkworms. Brought to North America for the same purpose, it has run wild across the continent.

habitat: Ground that ranges from swamps and stream bottoms to dry uplands, scattered among other hardwoods rather than in stands, in climates averaging about 50 inches of rain a year. It grows best on lower slopes and terraces in the Southeast.
distribution: From southwestern Maine west through New York, southern Ontario and central Michigan to Illinois and central Missouri, and south to eastern Oklahoma, eastern Texas and southern Florida, with local stands in central and southern Mexico. In Vermont it grows wild in a few swamps in the south of the state.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: A small understory tree of mountain forests, in the shade of taller trees along streams and on moist slopes.
distribution: Wild in Japan, Korea and eastern China.

habitat: Rocky slopes and thickets, where it is now rare.
distribution: Wild only in a few places in eastern China, in Zhejiang and Hubei.

habitat: Dry, sandy and gravelly soils, often in pure stands after fire, in a climate of cool to warm summers, cold winters and modest rain, 20 to 40 inches a year.
distribution: A narrow belt some 1,500 miles long and 500 wide around the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence, nearly all of it on ground glaciated in the last ice age: from Cape Breton Island, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, southern Quebec and Maine west to central Ontario and southeastern Manitoba, and south to the Great Lakes states, northern New England and Pennsylvania.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Dry, sandy uplands, oak savannas and open woods.
distribution: Wild in the western Great Lakes region, from Michigan and Ontario to Minnesota and Iowa.

habitat: Lowlands, hills and low mountains in temperate climates, often as an understory tree of oak and beech forests; one of the few strongly shade-tolerant trees native to Europe, though a little less so than beech. It prefers deep, moist, well-drained soils, never acid, and is hardy enough to grow in frost hollows; summer heat limits it in the south.
distribution: Southern Europe except Iberia, central Europe north to southern England and southern Sweden, and east around the Black Sea to the Caucasus and northern Iran, from sea level to about 2,300 feet in central Europe and 5,900 feet in Iran.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Mixed mountain forests.
distribution: Wild in southeastern Europe and western Asia, from the Balkans through Turkey to the Caucasus and northern Iran.

habitat: Mostly hill and mountain woods on moist, fertile soils, often along streams.
distribution: Wild across most of Europe, from Ireland and Scandinavia to the Urals, and in western Asia. It reaches farther north and west than any other European elm.

habitat: Along rivers and in dry valleys; where it has run wild, along streams and in grasslands.
distribution: Wild in western and central Asia, from Turkey and Iran to China. Planted in North America for windbreaks, it has run wild in the West, and is marked invasive in Vermont.

habitat: Moist mountain forests at middle and high elevations, often with oriental spruce and beech.
distribution: Wild in the mountains around the Black Sea, in the western Caucasus and across northern Turkey, west to Mount Ida near the Aegean.

habitat: The edges of woods, rocky slopes and dunes, and along streams.
distribution: Wild across much of the eastern and central United States and into Mexico, from southern Ontario and New York to Florida and Arizona.

habitat: Mixed forests along rivers and on mountain slopes.
distribution: Wild in northeastern China, Korea and the Russian Far East.

habitat: Old fields, fencerows and woodland edges in a humid climate with 30 to 55 inches of rain a year and 160 to 300 frost-free days; it spreads by suckers into thickets.
distribution: From southwestern Maine west through New York, southern Ontario and central Michigan; southwest through Illinois and Missouri to eastern Oklahoma and eastern Texas; and east to central Florida. It has died out in southeastern Wisconsin but is spreading into northern Illinois. In Vermont it grows wild only in the south of the state.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Open woods, thickets and woodland edges, often on limestone.
distribution: Wild in southern and central Europe and western Asia, from France and Italy to the Caucasus.

habitat: Swamps, bays and streamsides, on wet, acid soils. In the north of its range it loses its leaves in winter; in the south it keeps them.
distribution: Wild on the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains from Massachusetts to Florida and Texas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Where it has escaped from orchards.
distribution: Probably not truly wild anywhere. It most likely arose as a hybrid around the Caspian and Black Seas, and grows across Europe, North Africa and western Asia.

habitat: Along rivers and on open ground, in dry country.
distribution: Wild in the drier parts of northern China, from Inner Mongolia to Gansu and Shaanxi, and in Korea.

habitat: A shade-tolerant small tree of old woodland and ancient hedgerows on heavy clay soils.
distribution: Wild in western and central Europe, from Britain and southern Sweden south to Spain and Italy and east to Poland and Romania.

habitat: Where winter rain and summer fog keep the forest damp year round.
distribution: Wild only in a narrow coastal strip about 750 km long, from the Chetco River in southwestern Oregon to southern Monterey County, California.

habitat: Scattered groves within mixed conifer forest, mostly between about 1,400 and 2,000 m.
distribution: Wild only on the western slope of the Sierra Nevada in California, in some 65 to 75 groves.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Rich, moist, well-drained upland soils: it is demanding of soil fertility. Its range spans climates from 90 to 270 frost-free days and 30 to 60 inches of rain a year. In Vermont a tree of mixed hardwood forest.
distribution: Eastern North America, from Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, to northern Florida, and west to eastern Minnesota and eastern Texas.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Mostly wet bottomland, where its parents grow together. Most planted trees are named selections of it. Planted, it does best in full sun to part shade, on clay, loam or sand, acid to neutral, and puts up with both wet spells and dry ones.
distribution: A natural hybrid of red and silver maple, found wild where the two meet in eastern North America.

habitat: Mostly an understory shrub of woods on chalk and limestone.
distribution: Wild in western and southern Europe, northwest Africa and southwest Asia.

habitat: Swamps, wet woods and streamsides.
distribution: Wild along the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, from southern Maine to Florida and Texas.

habitat: A small understory tree of moist woods and forest edges.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland west to Manitoba and Minnesota and south to northern Florida and Mississippi. Native to Vermont.

habitat: The understory of hardwood forest.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Nova Scotia to Minnesota and south to Florida and Texas. Native to Vermont.

habitat: It climbs trees, rocks and walls in woodland. Where it has escaped from gardens in North America, it smothers trees and ground.
distribution: Wild across most of Europe and into western Asia; escaped in many places in North America.

habitat: Mountain slopes, scrub and rocks, between about 300 and 1,300 m.
distribution: Wild only in central China, where it is rare.

habitat: Moist, rich woods and streamsides.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Maine and Ontario to Kansas and south to Florida and Texas.
Its only wild populations are in Sichuan, in southern China; it reached Japan long ago and was grown there for fibre, which is why it was once thought Japanese.

habitat: Mountain thickets.
distribution: Wild in Japan, eastern China and Taiwan.

habitat: Hedges and open woods; in North America, woods it has invaded.
distribution: Wild across Europe, northwest Africa and western Asia. Brought to North America as a hedge, it is now invasive across the Northeast and Midwest, Vermont included.

habitat: Rocky hills. Found in the wild elsewhere mostly near past or present homes.
distribution: Wild only in the southern Balkan Peninsula, in Serbia, North Macedonia, Bulgaria and nearby; grown far beyond it.

habitat: Mostly moist bottomland and streamsides, in climates from warm and humid in the Southeast to cold and dry in the northwest. Dutch elm disease has killed most of the large trees.
distribution: Throughout eastern North America, from Cape Breton Island west through central Ontario to southern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan; south through eastern Montana, Wyoming, Nebraska, Kansas and Oklahoma into central Texas; east to central Florida, and north along the whole east coast.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Moist, rich soils of slopes and stream banks.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from southern Quebec and Maine to Florida and west to the Dakotas and Texas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Often dry, poor upland soils and ridges.
distribution: Wild across the eastern United States, from southern Maine to Florida and west to Minnesota and Texas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Dry, sandy or gravelly upland ridges and slopes.
distribution: Wild from southern Maine to Georgia and west to the Ohio Valley.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Dry, rocky ridges and upper slopes where few other oaks do well.
distribution: Wild from southern Maine and New York south along the Appalachians to Georgia.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: It springs up after fire and logging and spreads by root suckers into large clones. It stands great extremes: in Montana it has lived through −70°F lows and 105°F highs; in the far north it grows only on the warmest ground free of permafrost.
distribution: The widest range of any native tree in North America, over 111 degrees of longitude and 48 of latitude: from Newfoundland and Labrador west along the northern limit of trees to northwestern Alaska, and south, mostly in the mountains, through the West to Arizona, Trans-Pecos Texas and Mexico.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Moist bottomland along rivers and streams, where it is among the fastest-growing native trees. It stands temperatures from −50 to 115°F, and in the driest parts of its range keeps close to water.
distribution: Along streams and bottomlands from southern Quebec west to North Dakota and southwestern Manitoba, south to central Texas and east to northwestern Florida and Georgia. It is absent from the higher Appalachians and, except along rivers, from much of Florida and the Gulf coast. In the west it blends into the plains cottonwood.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: One of the first trees to come up after fire or clearcutting, and short-lived.
distribution: Wild across Canada and the northern United States, south in the Appalachians.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Stream banks, floodplains and lake shores, wherever the ground stays wet.
distribution: The largest native willow, wild across eastern North America.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Dry, sandy or rocky soils: the pine of the New Jersey Pine Barrens. It can sprout again from the trunk after fire, which few pines can.
distribution: Wild from central Maine to Georgia.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: A small tree of open woods, steppe edges and river valleys.
distribution: Wild from central and southeastern Europe to western Asia.

habitat: Pastures, open woods and thickets.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Ontario to Florida and Texas.

habitat: A tree of lowlands and lower hill slopes, in mixed woods on rich, often limy soils and on rocky slopes.
distribution: A smaller, patchier range than littleleaf linden's, reaching a little farther south but north only to southern Sweden: from Spain and southern England east to the Black Sea, with outlying stands in Turkey and the Caucasus.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Dry plains and steppe; where it has spread, fields and roadsides.
distribution: Wild in Mongolia, northern China, Korea and Central Asia. Planted across the American Plains for its hardiness, it is invasive in many states.

habitat: Planted for centuries around temples and along streets.
distribution: Wild in China; despite the name it reached Japan through cultivation.

habitat: A riverside tree of temperate climates with mild winters and warm summers broken by short dry spells, along rivers and in wet meadows.
distribution: Throughout Europe except the far north, north to the British Isles and the eastern Baltic, south around the Mediterranean to Morocco and Algeria, and east through Asia Minor and central Russia to the borders of China. Grown for so long that its natural range is hard to pin down, it was brought to North America in colonial times and has naturalized along streams.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: The hardiest and most northerly of its genus: in the Alps it grows higher than any other broadleaf tree, to about 6,600 feet, and in the south of its range it keeps to the mountains, though it stands hot summers too. It takes many soils, in damp woods, along streams and at forest edges, and spreads from bent-down branches and basal shoots into thickets.
distribution: The most widespread of all the cherries: through northern Europe and Central Asia east to Siberia, northern China and Japan, north to the shores of the Arctic Ocean, and south, in outlying stands, to Morocco.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Mountain forests. Most planted Japanese cherries are cultivars of it or its hybrids, selected over centuries for their blossom.
distribution: Wild in Japan, Korea and China.

habitat: A small tree of woodland edges and thickets in hills and low mountains.
distribution: Wild in Japan, Korea and southern China.

habitat: Along rivers and in mixed forest.
distribution: Wild in Korea and along both banks of the Amur River, in Manchuria and the Russian Far East.

habitat: River flats and moist lowland.
distribution: Wild across the boreal forest of Canada and Alaska and south into the northern United States, Vermont included.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Grown since ancient times; it escapes to hedgerows and old fields.
distribution: Descended from wild pears of Europe and western Asia.

habitat: Nutrient-rich soils, often in shady, moist hollows of mixed woods, mostly in hills and mountains; it cannot thrive where droughts are common. Its young trees grow well in shade, which lets it make its way into established forest.
distribution: Central and eastern Europe and the mountains of southern Europe, the Apennines and the Dinaric Alps, to the Caucasus and northern Turkey, north to southern Denmark. Planted heavily since the 1700s, in Britain and elsewhere, it has spread far beyond that range.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Where it has run wild: cracks in pavement, vacant lots and roadsides.
distribution: Wild in northern and central China and Taiwan. Brought to Philadelphia in 1784 and planted as a city tree, it is now invasive across much of the United States.

habitat: Along rivers and lakes and in wet woods, on many soils, even poor sands and gravels, as long as water is plentiful; it does poorly on chalky soils. It takes a wide range of temperatures and is fairly frost-hardy, usually growing below about 3,300 feet. It has naturalized in the northeastern United States, along streams and in wetlands.
distribution: Most of Europe, from Scandinavia, where it reaches about 65°N, to the Mediterranean and parts of North Africa, its spread east held back by dry country; the range map shows it reaching western Siberia and southwest Asia.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Moist bottomland and streamsides.
distribution: Wild in the Midwest and the Ohio Valley, from western Pennsylvania and southern Michigan west to Iowa and south to eastern Kansas, Oklahoma and Tennessee.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Mostly moist bottomland soils rich in lime. Often treated as a variety of sugar maple.
distribution: Wild from Vermont and southern Ontario west to Minnesota and south to Tennessee.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Planted for its flowers; where it has escaped, it is invasive.
distribution: Wild from Iran across southern Asia to China and Korea; escaped across the southeastern United States.

habitat: Woodland edges and open woods.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Minnesota and south in the Appalachians to Georgia. Native to Vermont.

habitat: High mountains, mostly above about 1,700 m (5,500 ft), where the balsam woolly adelgid has killed most of the mature trees.
distribution: Wild only in the high southern Appalachians of Virginia, North Carolina and Tennessee.
source: Fire Effects Information System (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Upland slopes and bottomland woods, best in a humid climate; one of the hardiest hickories, it grows under 30 to 80 inches of rain a year and from almost no snow to 100 inches or more.
distribution: Most of the eastern United States, from southeastern Nebraska and Minnesota through southern Ontario and Quebec to southern Maine, and south to Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and eastern Texas, with outlying stands in the mountains of northeastern Mexico. It is largely absent from the southeastern coastal plain and the lower Mississippi delta. Native to Vermont.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: The shady understory of rich bottomland woods, often in patches from root suckers.
distribution: Wild in the eastern United States, from western New York and southern Ontario to Florida and west to Nebraska and Texas.

habitat: Moist bottomland and rich slopes.
distribution: Wild from southern Quebec and New England to Florida and west to Minnesota and Texas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Along streams.
distribution: Wild in a small area of the Gulf states (Georgia, Florida, Alabama and Mississippi); planted and naturalized far beyond.

habitat: Mostly bottomland along rivers.
distribution: Wild in the southeastern United States, from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas and Kansas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Mostly dry ridges and upland slopes in oak-hickory forest.
distribution: Wild across the eastern United States, from southern New England and Ontario to Florida and west to Illinois and Texas.

habitat: Mountain forests. Resistant to chestnut blight, it has been crossed with American chestnut in the effort to bring that tree back.
distribution: Wild in China, Korea and Taiwan.

habitat: Rich, well-drained soils of slopes and stream terraces, in climates from New Brunswick's to Alabama's, with 25 to 80 inches of rain a year. Butternut canker has killed most of the wild trees.
distribution: From southeastern New Brunswick through New England, except northwestern Maine and Cape Cod, south to northern Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi and Arkansas, and west to central Iowa and Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Ontario and Quebec. Native to Vermont.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Old fields, open woods and bottomland.
distribution: Wild from Connecticut and southern New York to Florida and west to Kansas and Texas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: The understory of moist mixed woods, and coastal dunes.
distribution: Wild from coastal Massachusetts to Florida and west to Missouri and Texas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Mountain forests; grown for its nuts since ancient times.
distribution: Native from the Balkans east through Central Asia to the Himalayas and southwest China. The range map also shades much of western and central Europe, where it has been planted for so long that it grows wild.

habitat: An understory shrub of woods and hedgerows, long coppiced for poles and grown for its nuts.
distribution: Wild across Europe and western Asia.

habitat: Mountain forests; planted around temples and shrines for centuries.
distribution: Endemic to Japan, and grown widely for timber in Japan and China.

habitat: Mixed woods on moist, rich soils: lowland forests in the north and west of its range, mountains farther south, up to 5,200 to 5,900 feet in the Pyrenees and Alps and 7,200 in Iran. Its seeds usually lie dormant two years before sprouting. Ash dieback, a fungal disease, has killed much of it since the 1990s.
distribution: Throughout Europe's temperate zone, from the Atlantic coast to the Volga, much as English oak's range runs, and in the east through Turkey and the Caucasus to northern Iran.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Limestone bluffs and rocky glades. Rare in the wild.
distribution: Wild in a few scattered places in the southern United States: Tennessee, Alabama, the Ozarks and the Edwards Plateau of Texas.

habitat: Mostly bogs and swamps, under extremely varied climates: record lows from −20 to −79°F across its range, and from 7 inches of rain a year at Fort Yukon, Alaska, to 55 in eastern Canada. It is the one conifer of the region that drops its needles each fall.
distribution: One of the widest ranges of any North American conifer: from Newfoundland and Labrador west along the northern limit of trees across the Continental Divide into Yukon and Alaska, and south to Minnesota, Wisconsin, northern Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and New England, Vermont included.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Old fields, dry rocky ground and limestone, in climates from 15 to 60 inches of rain a year; summer rain may matter more to it than the yearly total. It spreads quickly into abandoned pasture.
distribution: The most widespread tree-sized conifer of the eastern United States, wild in every state east of the 100th meridian and north into southern Ontario and Quebec. Seedlings from planted trees have spread it well beyond, especially on the Great Plains.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Bottomland.
distribution: Wild originally only in the Red River country of Oklahoma, Texas and Arkansas. Planted across the Plains as thorny living fences before barbed wire, it has naturalized far beyond.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Cool, moist sites, mostly in the mountains, on rich slopes, in a humid to subhumid climate with 35 to 80 inches of rain a year. The hardiest of the native tree magnolias.
distribution: Widely distributed but never abundant, from western New York and southern Ontario southwest through Ohio, Indiana, Illinois and Missouri to southeastern Oklahoma and Louisiana; east to northwestern Florida and central Georgia; and north in the mountains to Pennsylvania.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Well-drained slopes in oak and pine woods.
distribution: Wild from southwestern Pennsylvania south through the Appalachians to northern Florida and west to Louisiana.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Moist bottomland and lower slopes. It hybridizes readily with the introduced white mulberry.
distribution: Wild across the eastern United States, from southern New England and Ontario to Florida and Texas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: The understory of rich, moist woods and ravines.
distribution: Wild in the Appalachians and the Ozarks, from southern Pennsylvania to Georgia and Arkansas.

habitat: Dry hillsides and open woods. Planted widely as a street tree, it seeds itself freely.
distribution: Wild in China and Korea; invasive in some southern states.

habitat: A cool, moist climate with 36 to 52 inches of rain a year, deep winter snow and only 90 to 150 frost-free days, on mountain slopes and in cool lowlands. In Vermont it is the spruce of the Green Mountains.
distribution: From the Maritime Provinces west to Maine, southern Quebec and southeastern Ontario, and south into New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Massachusetts; and along the high Appalachians through western Maryland, West Virginia and Virginia to western North Carolina and eastern Tennessee.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

habitat: Along rivers and on damp ground. Long planted in North America, it spreads by root suckers.
distribution: Wild from the Atlas Mountains of North Africa through southern and central Europe into Central Asia and western China.

habitat: Dry, poor, rocky or sandy uplands.
distribution: Wild across the southeastern and central United States, from southern New England to Florida and west to Kansas and Texas.
Domesticated in China several thousand years ago from wild trees of northwest China; the name persica comes from its arrival in Europe by way of Persia.

habitat: Along rivers, in dry country. Most weeping willows planted in the North are its hardier hybrids.
distribution: Wild in dry parts of northern China, Korea, Mongolia, Japan and Siberia. Grown for millennia across Asia, it reached Europe along the Silk Road.

habitat: Hill forests. Planted in the eastern United States for wildlife, it has escaped in places.
distribution: Wild across eastern Asia, from the Himalayas to China, Korea and Japan.

habitat: Thickets and woodland edges. Its purple-leaved selections are common street trees.
distribution: Wild in southeastern Europe and western Asia, from the Balkans to the Caucasus and Central Asia.

habitat: The understory of moist, rich woods along streams.
distribution: Wild only in a small area of the Southeast, nearly all of it in Alabama, with a little in southwest Georgia.

habitat: The understory of moist woods, and streamsides.
distribution: Wild across the southeastern United States, from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas.

habitat: Bogs, wet woods and dry rocky ground.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Minnesota and south to the Appalachians. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Planted widely as a hedge, it has spread through woods, and is banned from sale in several states as invasive.
distribution: Wild in Japan and eastern China; escaped across the Northeast, Vermont included.

habitat: Moist woods, streamsides and wooded hillsides.
distribution: Wild in the southeastern United States, from Virginia to Florida and west to Mississippi.

habitat: Swamps, pond edges and streams, often standing in water.
distribution: Wild across eastern and southern North America, from Nova Scotia to Florida and west to California. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Dry steppe and riverbanks. Planted across the Canadian Prairies for shelterbelts, it has escaped in places.
distribution: Wild in Siberia, Mongolia and northern China.

habitat: Thickets, old fields and woodland edges.
distribution: Wild across northeastern North America, from Maine and southern Quebec to Minnesota and south to Virginia and Oklahoma. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Wet thickets, streamsides and swamps.
distribution: Wild across most of northern North America, from Newfoundland to Alaska and south in the mountains. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Dry, rocky ground and open woods.
distribution: Wild across northeastern North America, from Newfoundland to Saskatchewan and south in the Appalachians. Native to Vermont.

habitat: Thickets and open woods. Planted widely for its red fall color, it has spread into woods and is banned from sale in several states, Vermont among them.
distribution: Wild in northeastern China, Korea and Japan; escaped across the eastern United States.

habitat: Woods, dry ridges and stream banks.
distribution: Wild only in the southern Appalachians, from North Carolina to Alabama.

habitat: Shaded, moist slopes and stream banks.
distribution: Wild across the eastern United States, from New York to Florida and west to Oklahoma.

habitat: Wooded slopes and bluffs, often over limestone.
distribution: Wild in the southeastern United States, from Tennessee and North Carolina to Florida and Louisiana.

habitat: Swamps, wet thickets and pond shores. A deciduous holly.
distribution: Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Minnesota and south to Florida. Native to Vermont.
